rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The correct sense of ‘bewitched’ is a person whose mind was confused by magic and displaced from its proper balance.
rows.anchor: والمسحور الذي قد سحر فاختلط عليه عقله وزال عن حد الاستواء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view takes ‘bewitched’ as corrupted, as spoiled food or land damaged by excessive rain.
rows.anchor: يقال : طعام مسحور إذا أفسد عمله وأرض مسحورة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda reads the phrase as ‘a human with a spleen,’ meaning a man with a lung.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : يريد بشرا ذا سحر

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba rejects Abu ʿUbayda’s strained reading because the early authorities gave clear interpretations.
rows.anchor: قال ابن قتيبة : ولا أدري ما الذي حمله على هذا التفسير المستكره

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses ‘bewitched’ as deceived: Quraysh alleged that people taught Muhammad words and tricked him, or that Satan made him mistake a devil for an angel.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : { مسحورا } أي مخدوعا لأن السحر حيلة وخديعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents compared Muhammad to a soothsayer, sorcerer, poet, teacher, and madman; they strayed from truth and could not find its path.
rows.anchor: فقالوا : إنه كاهن وساحر وشاعر ومعلم ومجنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an moves from theology and prophethood to objections about resurrection; its four central questions are divinity, prophecy, resurrection, and decree.
rows.anchor: مدار القرآن على المسائل الأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents present Muhammad’s claim that decayed bones return alive and rational as further evidence, in their view, that he was deranged.
rows.anchor: أنه يدعي أن الإنسان بعدما يصير عظاما ورفاتا فإنه يعود حيا عاقلا كما كان

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi defines ‘rafāt’ as fragments crushed by hand and gives examples from bones, gravel, and fine straw; it names broken particles.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي رحمه الله : الرفت كسر الشيء بيدك

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash gives the morphology ‘rafata, yaftu’ and treats rafāt and hutām as nouns for broken remains, like other fragment nouns.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش : رفت رفتا ، / فهو مرفوت نحو حطم حطما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection is that bodily elements scatter and mix with the world’s water, earth, air, and fire, making their exact reunion and revival seem impossible.
rows.anchor: فكيف يعقل اجتماعها بأعيانها مرة أخرى . وكيف يعقل عود الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection fails if God knows every particular and can do all possible things: the scattered parts remain distinct in His knowledge, and He can reassemble and revive them.
rows.anchor: هذه الأجزاء وإن اختلطت بأجزاء العالم إلا أنها متمايزة في علم الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stone and iron are more incompatible with life than bones because they were never parts of a living body; God can restore life even if the body becomes either.
rows.anchor: المنافاة بين الحجرية والحديدية وبين قبول الحياة أشد من المنافاة بين العظمية وبين قبول الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rational proof is that these bodies accepted life and intellect initially, and God knows each person’s parts and can do every possible thing, so their revival remains possible.
rows.anchor: قابلة للحياة والعقل إذ لو لم يكن هذا القبول حاصلا لما حصل العقل والحياة لها في أول الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Become stone or iron’ is not a literal command; it means that even such a transformation would not make people escape God’s power to resurrect them.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد منه الأمر بل المراد أنكم لو كنتم كذلك لما أعجزتم الله تعالى عن الإعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Or another creation’ means any state still farther from life than stone or iron; no particular substance needs to be identified because God can revive them in any state.
rows.anchor: فلا حاجة إلى أن يتعين ذلك الشيء ، لأن المراد أن أبدان الناس وإن انتهت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas interprets the impossible state as death itself, from which God would still restore life.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : المراد منه الموت ، يعني لو صارت أبدانكم نفس الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi says Ibn ʿAbbas’s reading is hyperbolic, since bodies are substances and death is an accident; moreover, one of two opposites cannot bear the other.
rows.anchor: أما في نفس الأمر فهذا محال ، لأن أبدان الناس أجسام والموت عرض

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the ‘other creation’ as heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد : يعني السماء والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer names the one who first created them: the argument for resurrection follows once they concede that God created living beings and remains capable and knowing.
rows.anchor: أن القول بصحة الإعادة فرع على تسليم أن خالق الحيوانات هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ explains ‘they will shake their heads’ as moving the head up and down; the ostrich is called nagḍ for this motion.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء يقال : أنغض فلان رأسه ينغضه إنغاضا إذا حركه

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham says a person shakes his head in rejection when told something, so the motion signals denial and incredulity.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الهيثم : يقال للرجل إذا أخبر بشيء فحرك رأسه إنكارا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their ‘when?’ question does not answer the rational proof that resurrection is possible; reason establishes possibility, while its timing can be known only through revelation.
rows.anchor: فأما أنه متى يوجد فذاك لا يمكن إثباته من طريق العقل ، بل إنما يمكن إثباته

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators take God’s ‘perhaps’ as certainty: resurrection is near.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون عسى من الله واجب معناه أنه قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that six hundred years have passed is answered by noting that if more time has elapsed than remains, the remainder is short and near.
rows.anchor: إذا كان ما مضى أكثر مما بقي كان الباقي قريبا قليلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The famous reading addresses unbelievers: ‘the day’ apposes to ‘near,’ referring to the final blast and a call summoning scattered bodies; the call is likened to other resurrection calls.
rows.anchor: انتصب يوما على البدل من قوله قريبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istijāba is a stronger form of answering than ijāba because it implies actively seeking to comply with the caller.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الاستجابة تقتضي طلب الموافقة فهي أوكد من الإجابة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says they emerge from graves, brush dust from their heads, and say ‘Glory and praise be to You.’
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير : يخرجون من قبورهم وينفضون التراب عن

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets ‘with His praise’ as their acknowledgment and obedience, though praise on that day will not benefit them.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة بمعرفته وطاعته

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: ‘Responding with praise’ can mean responding while praising, as in idioms describing someone arriving angry or carrying a sword; al-Kashshaf calls it a circumstantial phrase and stresses their submission.
rows.anchor: أي تستجيبون حامدين كما يقال : جاء بغضبه أي جاء غضبان

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say they praise God when praise can no longer benefit them; the image also functions as a threat.
rows.anchor: حمدوا حين لا ينفعهم الحمد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reads their brief stay as the interval between the two blasts, when punishment is lifted, linking their words in Yā Sīn.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس يريد بين النفختين الأولى والثانية

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the resurrection seems near: worldly life feels as if it had just vanished and the next life had always been present.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : معناه تقريب وقت البعث فكأنك بالدنيا لم تكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation makes the short stay the time spent on the gathering plain, since the final destination in Hell makes that interval seem brief.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد استقلال لبثهم في عرصة القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second, plausible reading ends the address to unbelievers at ‘near’ and addresses believers afterward, since their grateful response suits believers better; the first reading remains more famous.
rows.anchor: والقول الأول هو المشهور ، والثاني ظاهر الاحتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes ‘My servants’ as believers, since that wording usually denotes them; the command is to present proofs in the best manner, without insult, as also taught in two other verses.
rows.anchor: القول الأول : أن المراد به المؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good argument avoids abuse because insults invite retaliation, anger, and alienation; calm proof can move hearts and achieve the aim.
rows.anchor: إذا وقع الاقتصار على ذكر الحجة بالطريق الأحسن / الخالي عن الشتم والإيذاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan incites conflict when an argument is mixed with obscenity, and his enmity toward humanity is ancient and clear.
rows.anchor: متى صارت الحجة مرة ممزوجة بالبذاءة صارت سببا لثوران الفتنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ‘My servants’ means believers, God may rescue them from Meccan unbelievers or let those opponents afflict them; the Prophet must preach without being their guardian or guarantor.
rows.anchor: والمراد بتلك الرحمة الإنجاء من كفار مكة وأذاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view addresses unbelievers: invite them gently by affirming that worship of the one God and belief in resurrection are better than their contrary doctrines, rather than clinging to ancestral error.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأنا قبل النظر في الدلائل والبينات نعلم بالضرورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second reading, God’s choice to guide or punish is hidden, so people should seek true religion; the Prophet should be gentle because leniency moves hearts.
rows.anchor: فاجتهدوا أنتم في طلب الدين الحق ، ولا تصروا على الباطل والجهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge covers all existent and nonexistent things, not only the people addressed, so He knows what suits each and has favored some prophets over others.
rows.anchor: علمه غير مقصور عليكم ولا على أحوالكم بل علمه متعلق بجميع الموجودات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning David’s book instead of his great kingship signals that prophetic preference concerns knowledge and religion rather than wealth or power.
rows.anchor: لم يذكر ما آتاه من الملك وذكر ما آتاه من الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation says the Psalms foretold Muhammad as the final prophet and his community as the best nation and heirs of the earth.
rows.anchor: كتب في الزبور أن محمدا خاتم النبيين وأن أمته خير الأمم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form ‘a Psalms’ magnifies its status: zabūr means a written book, and indefiniteness presents it as a complete book.
rows.anchor: فكان معناه الكتاب فكان معنى التنكير أنه كامل في كونه كتابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation says Quraysh relied on Jews who denied any prophet or book after Moses; David’s Psalms refute that claim, and Hamza reads zabūran with ḍamma on zāy.
rows.anchor: واليهود كانوا يقولون : إنه لا نبي بعد موسى ولا كتاب بعد التوراة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse rebuts polytheists who claimed they were unworthy to worship God and instead worshipped angels through images; the referents cannot be idols because they seek nearness to God.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد الأصنام لأنه تعالى قال في صفتهم : { أولئك الذين يدعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports place the occasion among angel worshippers, worshippers of Christ and Ezra, or people who continued worshipping jinn after those jinn had accepted Islam.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنها نزلت في الذين عبدوا المسيح وعزيرا ، وقيل : إن قوما عبدوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says every Qur’anic use of ‘they claimed’ denotes a lie.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : كل موضع في كتاب الله تعالى ورد فيه لفظ زعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument is that a deity must remove harm and provide benefit, but angels, jinn, Christ, and Ezra cannot do so and therefore are not gods.
rows.anchor: الإله المعبود هو الذي يقدر على إزالة الضرر ، وإيصال المنفعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says lack of answered prayers does not prove angels powerless, since Muslims also pray to God without always receiving an answer; each side attributes effects to a different agent.
rows.anchor: قد نرى أيضا أن المسلمين يتضرعون إلى الله تعالى فلا تحصل الإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer is that polytheists admitted angels are God’s servants and that their creator must be greater; God’s known, complete power makes worship of Him preferable to worship of angels whose power is uncertain.
rows.anchor: كمال قدرة الله تعالى معلوم متفق عليه ، وكمال قدرة الملائكة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا المتكلمون
rows.claim: Sunni theologians offer a second proof: only God brings things from nonexistence to existence, so only He can harm or benefit and deserves worship.
rows.anchor: لا موجد إلا الله تعالى ولا مخرج لشيء من العدم إلى الوجود إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This proof does not work for Muʿtazilites, who allow people to originate their acts and thus cannot show that angels lack power to give life, cause death, or create bodies.
rows.anchor: كون العبد موجدا لأفعاله امتنع عليهم الاستدلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taḥwīl means transfer from one state or place to another; the verb is used for moving something and its being moved.
rows.anchor: والتحويل عبارة عن النقل من حال إلى حال ومكان إلى مكان

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ assigns ‘they worship’ to the human worshippers and ‘they seek’ to the worshipped beings; the latter seek provision and protection from God, proving their need and making God the proper object of worship.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء قوله : { يدعون } فعل الآدميين العابدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if angels were not acknowledged as needing mercy, they must be either self-existent, which pagans deny, or contingent and therefore dependent on God for their essence and perfections.
rows.anchor: إما أن يقال : إنها واجبة الوجود لذواتها ، أو يقال : ممكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies those worshippers as the prophets of 17:55: even the most honored prophets seek only God, so people should follow them and worship no other.
rows.anchor: هم الأنبياء الذين ذكرهم الله تعالى بقوله : { ولقد فضلنا بعض النبيين

rows.speaker: القائلون بهذا القول
rows.claim: Supporters object that angels do not fear punishment because they do not disobey, so the description fits prophets instead.
rows.anchor: الملائكة لا يعصون الله فلا يخافون عذابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi answers that angels would fear God’s punishment if they sinned, as the warning about any angel claiming divinity shows.
rows.anchor: الملائكة يخافون عذاب الله لو أقدموا على الذنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s punishment deserves to be feared even when some people fail to fear it through ignorance.
rows.anchor: فالمراد أن من حقه أن يحذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every village and its inhabitants will end in destruction or punishment, as follows from the preceding warning that God’s punishment must be feared.
rows.anchor: بين أن كل قرية مع أهلها فلا بد وأن يرجع حالها إلى أحد أمرين

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil says a righteous village is ended by death, while an unrighteous one is punished.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : أما الصالحة فبالموت ، وأما الطالحة فبالعذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view restricts the verse to unbelieving towns: they face total destruction or a lesser severe punishment such as killing leaders, Muslim conquest, captivity, seized property, and tribute.
rows.anchor: إما الاستئصال بالكلية وهو المراد من الإهلاك أو بعذاب شديد دون ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written decree means the stated outcome is certain and will occur.
rows.anchor: ثم بين تعالى أن هذا الحكم حكم مجزوم به واقع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion shifts from refuting polytheism and warning to prophethood because Quraysh demanded overwhelming miracles, including signs like earlier messengers received.
rows.anchor: كفار قريش اقترحوا من رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إظهار معجزات عظيمة قاهرة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr reports that Quraysh cited earlier prophets’ control of wind and revival of the dead and demanded comparable miracles.
rows.anchor: وعن سعيد بن جبير أن القوم قالوا : إنك تزعم أنه كان قبلك أنبياء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Meccans asked for Ṣafā to become gold and mountains to be removed for farming; God offered this with destruction as the condition for disbelief, but Muhammad chose to give them more time.
rows.anchor: روى ابن عباس أن أهل مكة سألوا الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يجعل لهم الصفا ذهبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that disbelieving after decisive miracles would make them liable to total destruction, which was withheld because God knew believers would emerge from them or their descendants.
rows.anchor: إنزال عذاب الاستئصال على هذه الأمة غير جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation is that their forebears had seen and rejected miracles, while the descendants merely imitated them and would likewise refuse belief.
rows.anchor: آباءكم الذين رأوها لم يؤمنوا بها وأنتم مقلدون لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third explanation is that God knew they would reject such signs too, so displaying them would be pointless and unbecoming of the wise.
rows.anchor: فعلم الله منكم أيضا أنكم لو شاهدتموها لكذبتم فكان إظهارها عبثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requested miracle would resemble the she-camel given to Thamūd: it was clear, yet they rejected it and incurred total destruction, so Quraysh should not demand signs capriciously.
rows.anchor: هي مثل آية ثمود ، وقد آتيناها ثمود

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ takes mubṣira to mean bright, as in the description of daylight in Yūnus.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : { مبصرة } أي مضيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second gloss is ‘possessing insight’: the sign lets anyone who reflects see guidance and infer the messenger’s truth.
rows.anchor: مبصرة } أي ذات أبصار أي فيها أبصار لمن تأملها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They wronged themselves by it’ means they harmed themselves through denial.
rows.anchor: فظلموا بها } أي ظلموا أنفسهم بتكذيبهم بها

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba glosses the phrase as denying that the sign came from God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة : { ظلموا * بها } أي جحدوا بأنها من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every sign warns of punishment, either immediate or in the next life; even the possibility that it is a miracle should frighten people into examining and reflecting on it.
rows.anchor: فلو لم يتفكروا فيها ولم يستدلوا بها على الصدق لاستحقوا العقاب الشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading says God’s wisdom and power encompass everyone, who remains under His control; this reassures Muhammad that God will support his mission.
rows.anchor: حكمته وقدرته محيطة بالناس فهم في قبضته وقدرته

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says God protected Muhammad from people trying to kill him, as the promise of protection also states.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن : حال بينهم وبين أن يقتلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes ‘the people’ as Meccans: God’s encompassing them means He will conquer and overcome them, as other verses promise.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالناس أهل مكة وإحاطة الله بهم هو أنه تعالى يفتحها للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report places the verse at Badr: while the armies approached, Muhammad prayed with Abu Bakr, then went out in armor urging the people with the promise of victory.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه لما تزاحف الفريقان يوم بدر ورسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في العريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view is Muhammad’s dream at Badr of Quraysh’s death sites; Quraysh mocked the fulfilled identifications and hurried the promised event.
rows.anchor: أن الله أرى محمدا في المنام مصارع كفار قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view is his dream of entering Mecca: at Ḥudaybiyya, ʿUmar worried it had not happened; Abu Bakr said no year was specified, and they entered the following year, fulfilling the vision.
rows.anchor: أن المراد رؤياه التي رآها أنه يدخل مكة وأخبر بذلك أصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that these two events occurred in Medina does not rule them out, since Muhammad could have seen them in a Meccan dream.
rows.anchor: وهذا السؤال ضعيف لأن هاتين الواقعتين مدنيتان أما رؤيتهما في المنام

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says Muhammad saw the Umayyads leaping like monkeys on his pulpit; Ibn ʿAbbas reports this from ʿAṭāʾ, and the vision grieved him.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن المسيب رأى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بني أمية ينزون

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi objects that this Umayyad interpretation concerns Medina although the sura is Meccan; Razi answers that Muhammad could have seen a future pulpit in Medina.
rows.anchor: والإشكال المذكور عائد فيه لأن هذه الآية مكية وما كان لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest view, held by most commentators, identifies the vision with the Night Journey; most see no linguistic distinction between a waking vision and a dream, while a minority takes the journey itself to have been a dream, which Razi rejects as false.
rows.anchor: والقول الرابع : وهو الأصح وهو قول أكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The journey became a trial because many believers disbelieved Muhammad after hearing it, while the sincere grew firmer in faith.
rows.anchor: كذبوه وكفر به كثير ممن كان آمن به وازداد المخلصون إيمانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax places the vision and the Qur’an’s cursed tree together as trials; most identify the tree as zaqqūm, whose mention challenged their assumptions about fire and trees.
rows.anchor: قالوا : إنها شجرة الزقوم المذكورة في القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zaqqūm caused two taunts: Abu Jahl asked how a tree could grow in fire that burns stone, and Ibn al-Zibaʿrā mocked it as dates with butter; another verse answers the objection.
rows.anchor: أن أبا جهل قال : زعم صاحبكم بأن نار جهنم تحرق الحجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Qur’an does not explicitly curse the tree, the phrase can refer to the curse on its eaters, to Arabs’ name for harmful food, or to the tree’s distance from every good quality.
rows.anchor: المراد لعن الكفار الذين يأكلونها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas identifies the cursed tree as the Umayyads, specifically al-Ḥakam ibn Abi al-ʿĀṣ, after Muhammad dreamed that Marwan’s descendants passed his pulpit among themselves.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما : الشجرة بنو أمية يعني الحكم

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says the Umayyad account is unlikely because it occurred in Medina whereas the sura is Meccan, unless this verse alone is considered Medinan.
rows.anchor: هذه القصة كانت بالمدينة ، والسورة مكية

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha’s rebuke to Marwan supports the curse interpretation, saying God cursed his father while Marwan was still in his loins.
rows.anchor: قول عائشة لمروان لعن الله أباك وأنت في صلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third view identifies the cursed tree as the Jews, linking it to the verse that says unbelievers were cursed.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث : أن الشجرة الملعونة في القرآن هي اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reason God withheld the requested miracles is that warnings about worldly and next-world punishment, including zaqqūm, only increased these people’s transgression; further signs would not help them and would be unwise.
rows.anchor: خوفوا بمخاوف الدنيا والآخرة وبشجرة الزقوم فما زادهم هذا التخويف إلا طغيانا كبيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Adam story connects in three ways: earlier prophets also suffered from their contemporaries; Quraysh’s pride and envy parallel Iblis’s causes of disbelief; and Iblis’s threat explains the great transgression just mentioned.
rows.anchor: فلأجل هذا المقصود ذكر الله تعالى قصة إبليس وآدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story appears in seven suras—al-Baqara, al-Aʿrāf, al-Ḥijr, this sura, al-Kahf, Ṭā Hā, and Ṣād—so its fuller discussion need not be repeated.
rows.anchor: هذه القصة قد ذكرها الله تعالى في سور سبعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi lists unresolved questions about whether all angels or only earthly angels were commanded to prostrate; the general wording suggests all, but another verse describing heavenly angels prostrating suggests an exception.
rows.anchor: العموم إلا أن قوله تعالى في آخر سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi lists debated issues: whether prostration was physical or a greeting, whether Adam or God was its object, whether Iblis was an angel and when he became an unbeliever, and when the angels prostrated.
rows.anchor: إن إبليس هل هو من الملائكة أم لا ؟ وإن لم يكن من الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other open questions concern Iblis’s argument, whether he knew God but became unbelieving from pride and envy or never knew God, and why God delayed and empowered him to tempt people.
rows.anchor: دلت هذه الآيات على أن إبليس كان عارفا بربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis’s refusal is followed by two statements: he denies serving one made from clay, arguing that his own origin is superior and the superior should not serve the inferior.
rows.anchor: وهذا استفهام بمعنى الإنكار معناه أن أصلي أشرف من أصله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains araytaka as ‘tell me’; Razi gives three grammatical readings of the following phrase: an elliptical question, an omitted interrogative, or a direct object with the kāf only for address.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : قوله { أرأيت } معناه أخبرني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the third parsing, Iblis asks in amazement whether God favored this one over him, implying that God should not have favored him if Iblis had seen or known him.
rows.anchor: أبصرت أو علمت هذا الذي كرمت علي

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the yāʾ in ‘if You delay me’ in both connected and pause forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير { لئن أخرتني إلى يوم القيامة } بإثبات الياء

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read the form without the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي بالحذف

rows.speaker: نافع وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Abu ʿAmr retain the yāʾ in connected recitation but omit it at pause.
rows.anchor: نافع وأبو عمرو بإثباته في الوصل دون الوقف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iḥtināk has two readings: seizing or consuming completely, or leading by a cord under an animal’s jaw; Abu Muslim uses the latter to mean controlling Adam’s descendants like a bridled horse.
rows.anchor: في الاحتناك قولان : أحدهما : أنه عبارة عن الأخذ بالكلية

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim derives iḥtināk from the jaw and reads it as possessing and leading people as a rider leads a horse with reins.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم : الأحتناك افتعال من الحنك كأنهم يملكهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The few exempt from Iblis’s reach are identified with God’s servants beyond his authority; Razi gives three explanations for Iblis’s accurate prediction: he heard the angels’ warning, saw Adam’s weak resolve, or understood the early dominance of lower faculties.
rows.anchor: إلا قليلا } هم الذين ذكرهم الله تعالى في قوله { إن عبادي ليس لك عليهم سلطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third explanation analyzes humans as animal appetite, predatory anger, demonic imagination, and angelic reason: the first three dominate early, while reason matures later.
rows.anchor: مركب من قوة بهيمية شهوانية ، وقوة سبعية غضبية ، وقوة وهمية شيطانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s ‘go’ means proceed with the course you chose, not literally move away; it releases Iblis and entrusts him to his chosen task.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس من الذهاب الذي هو نقيض المجيء وإنما معناه امض لشأنك الذي اخترته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Your reward’ uses a plural address by combining the follower’s punishment with Iblis’s; alternatively it shifts address to the absent, or singles Iblis out because each later sinner’s burden also falls on the originator of that sin.
rows.anchor: فإن جهنم جزاؤهم وجزاؤكم ثم غلب المخاطب على الغائب فقيل جزاؤكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says whoever establishes an evil practice bears its sin and the sins of everyone who follows it, explaining Iblis’s shared punishment.
rows.anchor: أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال من سن سنة سيئة فعليه وزرها ووزر من عمل بها إلى يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawfūr can mean made full or abundant; on the first derivation the punishment is fully supplied, and on the second it is plentiful. The word jazāʾ is an accusative verbal noun.
rows.anchor: أما المتعدي فيقال : وفرته أفره وفرا

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s line uses yufrihi to witness the transitive sense of making something abundant.
rows.anchor:
قال زهير
ومن يجعل المعروف من دون عرضه … يفره ومن لا يتق الشتم يشتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God first grants Iblis respite until the appointed time, then commands him to try to unsettle whoever he can; istifzāz means startling or agitating, and the imperative is a threat.
rows.anchor: يقال أفزه الخوف واستفزه أي أزعجه واستخفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s ‘voice’ means his call to disobedience; another interpretation takes it as singing, entertainment, and play.
rows.anchor: وصوته دعاؤه إلى معصية الله تعالى ، وقيل : أراد بصوتك الغناء واللهو واللعب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ derives ajlib from clamor and explains it as shouting against them.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : إنه من الجلبة وهو الصياح

rows.speaker: الليث وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Al-Layth and Abu ʿUbayda say ajlabū and jalabū both mean to shout.
rows.anchor: قال الليث وأبو عبيدة أجلبوا وجلبوا من الصياح

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ajlaba ʿalā al-ʿaduww means to gather cavalry against an enemy; on this reading gather every available scheme against them, with the bāʾ in ‘with your cavalry’ extra.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج في فعل وأفعل ، أجلب على العدو إجلابا إذا جمع عليه الخيول

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit says the phrase can mean that Satan’s forces help one another against people; its object is omitted and the cavalry and foot soldiers are the means.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السكيت يقال هم يجلبون عليه بمعنى أنهم يعينون عليه

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī says the verb can mean to threaten someone with evil and rally a force against him.
rows.anchor: روى ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي أجلب الرجل على الرجل إذا توعده الشر

rows.speaker: أبو الضحى عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Ḍuḥā reports Ibn ʿAbbas’s view that every rider or walker engaged in disobedience belongs to Iblis’s cavalry and troops.
rows.anchor: أبو الضحى عن ابن عباس أنه قال : ( كل راكب أو راجل في معصية الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other views posit mounted and walking troops of devils or take the phrase as a figure for using all one’s force; Razi says the figurative reading is closest.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث : أن المراد منه ضرب المثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khayl can mean horsemen or horses, but here it means horsemen; rajil is the plural of rāجل, with Ḥafṣ reading the jīm with kasra and others with ḍamma.
rows.anchor: والمراد ههنا الأول والرجل جمع راجل

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd says rajul and rajil are equivalent forms, like several other paired forms.
rows.anchor: قال أبو زيد يقال رجل ورجل بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: ثعلب عن الفراء
rows.claim: Thaʿlab reports from al-Farrāʾ that rajul, rajil, and rajulān have the same meaning.
rows.anchor: ثعلب عن الفراء قال : يقال رجل ورجل ورجلان بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Sharing wealth with Satan covers every wrongful handling of money, whether acquired unlawfully or spent unlawfully, including usury, usurpation, theft, and invalid transactions; Razi endorses this broad definition.
rows.anchor: كل تصرف قبيح في المال سواء كان ذلك القبيح بسبب أخذه من غير حقه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says sharing wealth means declaring certain livestock forbidden as baḥīra or sāʾiba.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : المشاركة في الأموال هي أن جعلوا بحيرة وسائبة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima says it means cutting the ears of livestock.
rows.anchor: عكرمة هي عبارة عن تبتيكهم آذان الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is assigning a portion of one’s wealth to beings besides God, as in the cited verse; Razi prefers the judge’s more comprehensive account.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي أن جعلوا من أموالهم شيئا لغير / الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Aṣamm objects that children are not blameworthy for their parents’ sexual sins; the response is that Satan shares in the means of producing the child through urging illicit sex.
rows.anchor: وزيف الأصم ذلك بأن قال إنه لا ذم على الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations of sharing in children include urging illicit sex, naming children servants of al-Lāt or al-ʿUzzā, and steering them toward false religions.
rows.anchor: أن يسموا أولادهم بعبد اللات وعبد العزى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Further interpretations include killing or burying children alive and teaching them obscene poetry, murder, fighting, and vile trades; the general rule includes any parental conduct that leads a child to wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: كل تصرف من المرء في ولده على وجه يؤدي إلى ارتكاب منكر أو قبيح فهو داخل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s promises work by denying any harm from sin—no resurrection, Paradise, Hell, or life after death—then by exaggerating worldly pleasure so that abstinence seems a loss.
rows.anchor: لا معاد ولا جنة ولا نار ، ولا حياة بعد هذه الحياة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poet’s couplet urges taking one’s share of pleasure because every pleasure eventually passes, illustrating Satan’s appeal to immediate enjoyment.
rows.anchor: خذوا بنصيب من سرور ولذة … فكل وإن طال المدى يتصرم
